$AAPL Apple shares are down nearly 4% in premarket trading after being roughly flat going into last night’s earnings call. What happened?

Apple doesn’t put guidance in its release, but on the call it guided to December-quarter revenue growth of 7% to 10%, above the 5.9% FactSet consensus, even as Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan expects memory-related supply constraints on Mac and iPad.

So far so good. But CFO Kevan Parekh then guided gross margin to 45% to 46%, citing higher memory costs and the Siri AI ramp. That’s below the 47% analysts expected, according to Bloomberg, and down from 47.9% in the fiscal fourth quarter. Relatedly he also expects higher margin Services growth to slow to 8% to 9%, short of the 10% analysts expected.

That matters at Apple’s valuation: the stock trades at 36 times next year’s expected earnings, with earnings growth of only 1% expected, per Oppenheimer’s Martin Yang in The Wall Street Journal. By my math, each point of gross margin on the guided revenue midpoint is worth about $0.09 a share in the December quarter, so falling 1 to 2 points short of the 47% estimate costs roughly $0.09 to $0.18 in EPS.

It sort of passed under the radar, but last week after 13 years the Bank of Japan says underlying inflation has finally reached its 2% target, the goal it set in January 2013 and once expected to hit in about two years. Still, the BOJ held at 1.25% on an 8-1 vote, with only hawk Takata dissenting for a hike, and Governor Ueda kept December firmly in play.

The new Outlook Report leans hawkish:
▪️ Core CPI forecast (ex-fresh food) for fiscal 2027 raised to 2.6% from 2.4%; fiscal 2026 unchanged at 2.5%
▪️ Ex-fresh food and energy peaks at 2.7% in fiscal 2027
▪️ Risks to prices judged skewed to the upside
▪️ Growth stuck around 0.7% a year
▪️ ETF sales nearly triple to about ¥860 billion a year, cutting the unwind to 43 years from 110+

The hold was even as the BOJ is still deeply accommodative. At 1.25%, the policy rate is about -1.35% in real terms against Tokyo’s 2.6% core reading.

 Bloomberg Economics sees hikes in December, March and July to 2%, the top of ING’s 1.75% to 2.00% neutral range. Even then, the real rate would be about -0.6% against the board’s own fiscal 2027 forecast.

For the yen, the Fed-BOJ gap is roughly half its mid-2024 level, yet the yen is only about 3% off its weakest levels. If both the Fed and the BOJ hike in December, the gap doesn’t narrow, which fits ING’s call for a 155 to 160 range.

It did not "interpret the raw weights," it looked at the outputs of Qwen 0.8B and noticed that it was repeating itself in a loop, causing it to make trivial errors on a math test, even when it was capable of solving the problem. 

Astra then used standard interpretability techniques to isolate the neuron most responsible for this looping behavior, and ablate that looping behavior from the model by subtracting that direction from the activations. This suppressed the looping and allowed it to output the right answers.

This technique would not work on a model that did not have such a trivially suppressible issue. You cannot use a technique like this to make a normal model smarter at math.

Counterpoint on $MRVL / $LITE acqusition:

- "Every buyer that competes with Marvell will want a second, independent laser source".

They identify $SIVE / Scintil Photonics as new CW / ELS capacity, with names like $CRDO as potential partners of Sivers.

- "With Lumentum sold out for years, the overflow goes to whoever has merchant capacity"

Already said this before, but we'll likely see some incentive to diversify laser sourcing. 

Sivers was cited here, and comes online with 100M lasers / external foundry capacity (2:1 external/internal target). 

To demonstrate the sheer scale on that, $AAOI exit 2026 laser capacity target was roughly ~24M/year (but different blend). 

- "Module makers move upstream" was also another second order effect. 

 $JBL as one example is now heavily competing with the combined Lumentum + Marvell.... There's other players like $SMTC that are explicitly doing M&A for expanding laser capacity.

I don't think the overall AI valuation crash is representative of individual company strength in the optical sector.

There's very compelling opportunities in the laser bottleneck in the upcoming year that I believe markets are mispricing.

everyone believes intelligence has unlimited demand, not just the maxis. but what the maxis get wrong is that the intelligence anthropic and openai and frontier models are building isn’t the generic kind you’re picturing. let me explain-

the two biggest uses of compute are crudely either training or inference. the “generic intelligence” everyone says has unlimited demand comes from mainly inference, and inference needs very different power and utilization than training. inference comes in bursts, so you have to by default overbuild capacity to handle the peaks until the utilization problem is solved, which means almost by definition we are going to overbuild. but training doesn’t have that problem: the workload is steady and the demand curve is knowable. so data centers end up overbuilt right now precisely because utilization isn’t optimized yet.

so anthropic and the other frontier labs are building their future on training, which is why they are saying they can soak up all this excess capacity. but their “intelligence” isn’t workplace productivity. it’s the leap toward singularity-type outcomes: new drug discoveries, cyber capabilities, recursive self-improvement. these are true 1-of-1s. that’s why when anthropic talks about “existential threats to humanity,” it isn’t talking about job losses, not really. it’s saying they’re on the precipice of unbelievable discoveries, because they’re still TRAINING MORE MODELS.

but distillation is real and open source is real. the half-life of any frontier model is tiny because nothing protects it the way IP protects a patent. imagine a rare disease drug company that spends billions on research, and two months after a breakthrough a generic shows up. that company can never recoup its investment, unless it can discover an infinite number of rare disease drugs. THAT is the kind of intelligence anthropic is betting on. that’s what the $800bn of compute spend is betting on.

so the questions you need to ask are: 1) if intelligence is two-tiered, what does each tier cost? what’s the cost of AGI, and what’s the cost of the generic intelligence that has infinite demand? and 2) are we allocating capital with the right risk curve and decay function to find out whether the AGI payoff is real? and if it is real, could a private company ever truly own it?

that’s the cognitive dissonance at the heart of this entire paradox: everyone is gaslighting each other about what intelligence is as the unit of measurement is purposely kept vague by both the users and the suppliers. generic intelligence has unlimited demand, but it’s a certain race to the bottom. "superintelligence" is the opposite: it can't have unlimited demand by definition, but if it delivers even half of what it promises, no private company will ever get to keep it, at least not without the government stepping in to guard the moat (which is why anthropic keeps playing this angle up, without having shown any demonstration they are near this level of discovery at all). and at that point you have to ask who is going to hold the bag, and whether that was in fact, very intelligent at all.

"superintelligence" is the opposite: it can't have unlimited demand by definition, but if it delivers even half of what it promises, no private company will ever get to keep it, at least not without the government stepping in to guard the moat (which is why anthropic keeps playing this angle up, without having shown any demonstration they are near this level of discovery at all). and at that point you have to ask who is going to hold the bag, and whether that was in fact, very intelligent at all.

Palantir, once again, puts up one of the best quarters that the market has ever seen.

Being able to grow revenues 96% while having 62% adjusted operating income margins is unheard of. There is no other software company that is even close to putting up these types of results.

US commercial revenue officially passed US government revenue for the first time. I remember in 2022, the bear case was centered around the company being too reliant on the USG. If anything, that was the bull case because that gave them the time to figure out how to scale US commercial and now we have a company doing 29% growth QoQ, which would be amazing YoY for most companies as Dr. Karp said, but also scaling that YoY growth at 148% for US commercial. 

It is unprecedented. 

So, why? Why is it happening? 

Well, it seems like Sovereignty is a very, very big deal.

“The Sovereign AI movement is imposing the most dramatic dichotomy between haves and have nots that I have witnessed in 30 years of business. Every institution—government and commercial—is rapidly being forced, voluntarily or not, into one of these two categories,” said Alex Karp.

Having been to multiple AIPCons and Institutional Sovereignty bootcamps this year, I can say that this is very real. When you talk to customers, you realize that they want much, much more than just plugging their enterprise into an LLM. They actually want FDEs, they want the grunt work of figuring out how to build custom workflows, they want the post training and fine tuning of open models...they want outcomes. The reason Palantir is growing this fast and continuing to show so much operating leverage is because they are delivering outcomes. That's why this is working. 

The company is doing this with 1090 customers. Most enterprise software companies at this scale have well over 100K customers. I mean, once again, this is unprecedented. Their net dollar retention scaled to 165%...their rule of 40 is now a new record at 158%...these are numbers that you only get when the company's entire mission is geared towards making sure their partners succeed and as a result, they are being paid for that value and then monetizing that value at the highest efficiency any software company ever has before with these margins. 

Stock is down due to macro, midterms, etc. but the core business is growing faster than anything we have ever seen and doing so in one of the most profitable ways ever. Their adjusted FCF in 90 days is now equal to the revenue they were bringing in early last year. 

An incredible quarter by Palantir, congrats to all shareholders and a deep thank you to the executive team and employees.
